title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip in System Design Interviews
summary: Ten database concepts every system design candidate must explain: indexing, transactions, ACID, isolation levels, locking, MVCC, connection pooling, partitioning, replication and sharding. Each has a worked example, its trade-offs and the interview takeaway.

chapters.title: 10 Database Concepts for System Design Interviews
points: Cover promise: the 10 database concepts interviewers probe, ordered from foundational to advanced
1. Indexing: make reads fast by avoiding full table scans
2. Transactions: group statements into one all-or-nothing unit
3. ACID: the four guarantees a transaction gives you
4. Isolation Levels: how much concurrent transactions can see of each other
5. Locking: shared and exclusive locks that serialize conflicting access
6. MVCC: readers see snapshots so they never block writers
7. Connection Pooling: reuse expensive database connections
8. Partitioning: split one big table into smaller pieces on one server
9. Replication: copy data to other nodes for availability and read scale
10. Sharding: spread data across independent servers to scale writes

chapters.title: Indexing
points: What it is: a separate sorted structure, usually a B-tree, that maps column values to row locations
Why it exists: without one, WHERE email = 'a@x.com' scans all 10M rows, O(n); a B-tree lookup is O(log n), about 3-4 page reads
Used for: WHERE filters, JOIN keys, ORDER BY, UNIQUE constraints and foreign keys
How it works: CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email); EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='a@x.com' flips from Seq Scan (about 1.2s) to Index Scan (about 0.1ms)
Composite index (country, created_at) serves WHERE country='IN' AND created_at > X, and country alone, but not created_at alone (leftmost-prefix rule)
Benefit: point and range lookups turn from linear scans into a few page reads
Benefit: a covering index holds every column the query needs, so it never touches the table (index-only scan)
Benefit: a UNIQUE index enforces uniqueness cheaply
Consider: every index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and uses disk, because each write also updates every index
Consider: low-cardinality columns (boolean, status) rarely benefit, and wrapping a column in a function (LOWER(email)) bypasses the index
Interview takeaway: index the columns you filter, join and sort on, put equality columns first, and verify with EXPLAIN; indexes trade write cost for read speed

chapters.title: Transactions
points: What it is: a group of reads and writes that the database treats as one logical unit that either fully commits or fully rolls back
Why it exists: a crash or error midway through a multi-step change would leave data half-updated and inconsistent
Used for: money transfers, order placement plus stock decrement, any multi-row invariant
How it works: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT; if the second UPDATE fails, ROLLBACK restores both rows
Under the hood, a write-ahead log (WAL) records changes before they are applied, so a commit survives a crash
Benefit: no partial failures, because the unit is atomic
Benefit: application code can reason about the state before and after, without handling every half-done case
Benefit: SAVEPOINTs allow partial rollback inside a long transaction
Consider: long transactions hold locks and bloat the log, so keep them short and never wait on user input or a remote API inside one
Consider: a transaction covers a single database only; across services you need sagas or two-phase commit
Interview takeaway: wrap multi-step invariants in a transaction, keep it short, and know it stops at the database boundary

chapters.title: ACID
points: What it is: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability, the four guarantees of a reliable transaction
Why it exists: it gives developers a predictable contract so correctness does not depend on timing or crashes
Used for: payments, inventory, bookings, and any system where wrong data costs money

How it works: transfer $100 from A to B. Atomicity: both updates or neither. Consistency: CHECK (balance >= 0) is never violated. Isolation: another transaction never sees A debited but B not yet credited. Durability: after COMMIT returns, a power cut cannot lose it, because the WAL was fsynced
Atomicity is implemented with undo logs or rollback; durability with the write-ahead log and fsync
Benefit: strong correctness guarantees on a single node
Benefit: simpler application code, because the database enforces the invariants
Benefit: crash recovery replays the WAL to a known good state
Consider: 'Consistency' in ACID (constraints hold) is not the 'Consistency' in CAP (all replicas agree)
Consider: strict isolation and fsync-per-commit cost throughput; many NoSQL stores relax ACID (BASE) to scale
Interview takeaway: be able to give a one-line example for each letter, and say that Isolation is the tunable one

chapters.title: Isolation Levels
points: What it is: a setting that controls which effects of concurrent transactions one transaction is allowed to see
Why it exists: full serializability is slow, so databases let you trade strictness for throughput
Used for: choosing per transaction, e.g. READ COMMITTED for ordinary web requests, SERIALIZABLE for financial ledgers
Anomalies: dirty read (see uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (same row changes between two reads), phantom read (a new row appears in a repeated range query)
Read Uncommitted allows all three; Read Committed blocks dirty reads; Repeatable Read also blocks non-repeatable reads; Serializable blocks phantoms too
How it works: T1 runs SELECT balance (100). T2 updates it to 50 and commits. T1 reads again. Under Read Committed T1 sees 50; under Repeatable Read T1 still sees 100
Defaults: PostgreSQL and Oracle use Read Committed; MySQL InnoDB uses Repeatable Read
Benefit: you can tune each workload, trading correctness against concurrency
Consider: higher levels cause more aborts or blocking, so be ready to retry serialization failures (Postgres error 40001)
Consider: write skew (two doctors both go off-call) slips past Repeatable Read and snapshot isolation; it needs Serializable or explicit locks
Interview takeaway: name the three anomalies, map them to the four levels, and say which default your database uses

chapters.title: Locking
points: What it is: a mechanism where a transaction claims a row, page or table so that conflicting access has to wait
Why it exists: two transactions updating the same row at once would produce lost updates
Used for: protecting inventory counts, seat bookings, balance updates and queue-claiming jobs
Lock modes: shared (S) lets many readers in; exclusive (X) lets one writer in and blocks everyone else

How it works: T1 runs SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id=7 FOR UPDATE and gets 1; T2 running the same query blocks until T1 commits; T1 sets stock=0 and commits; T2 then reads 0 and refuses the sale, so no oversell
Pessimistic locking: lock first, then work (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE). Optimistic: UPDATE ... WHERE id=7 AND version=3, then retry if 0 rows were updated
Benefit: it guarantees exclusive access to a critical row and prevents lost updates
Benefit: optimistic locking has no waiting and suits low-contention workloads
Consider: deadlocks, where T1 waits for T2 and T2 for T1; the DB kills one victim, so acquire locks in a consistent order and retry
Consider: lock escalation and long-held locks reduce concurrency; SKIP LOCKED helps job queues
Interview takeaway: use pessimistic locks for high contention and optimistic versioning for low contention; always mention deadlock handling

chapters.title: MVCC
points: What it is: Multi-Version Concurrency Control, where the database keeps several versions of a row and each transaction reads a consistent snapshot
Why it exists: with plain locking, readers block writers and writers block readers, which kills throughput
Used for: PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB and Oracle, which implement snapshot reads under Read Committed and Repeatable Read
How it works: an UPDATE does not overwrite; it creates a new row version tagged with its transaction id (Postgres xmin/xmax). A reader that began at txid 100 only sees versions committed before it
Example: T1 (txid 100) reads price=10; T2 (txid 101) updates price to 12 and commits; T1 still reads 10, because version 12 is newer than its snapshot
Benefit: readers never block writers and writers never block readers
Benefit: consistent, repeatable reads without read locks
Benefit: long reports run on a stable snapshot while writes continue
Consider: old versions pile up as dead rows; Postgres needs VACUUM, InnoDB purges its undo log, and long transactions stop the cleanup
Consider: writers still conflict with each other and still need row locks, and snapshot isolation allows write skew
Interview takeaway: MVCC trades extra storage and cleanup work for non-blocking reads, and it is why Postgres read-heavy workloads scale

chapters.title: Connection Pooling
points: What it is: a cache of open database connections that the application borrows and returns instead of opening a new one per request
Why it exists: a new connection costs a TCP + TLS + auth handshake (tens of ms) and a server process or thread (Postgres uses about 10MB per connection)
Used for: web backends, serverless functions and any service with many short queries
How it works: pool size 20. A request borrows a connection, runs its query in 3ms and returns it. 1,000 requests per second share 20 connections instead of opening 1,000
Tools: HikariCP (Java), pgbouncer (Postgres proxy), RDS Proxy; pgbouncer transaction mode hands a connection out only for the length of one transaction
Benefit: removes connection setup latency from the request path
Benefit: caps the connection count, so the database is not overwhelmed (Postgres max_connections default is 100)
Benefit: gives backpressure, because excess requests queue instead of crashing the database
Consider: a pool that is too big causes contention; a pool that is too small causes timeouts; start near (cores x 2) + disks
Consider: leaked connections (never returned) drain the pool, and session state like SET or prepared statements breaks in transaction pooling mode
Interview takeaway: say the database has a connection limit, so you put a pool or proxy in front and size it deliberately, especially with serverless or many app instances

chapters.title: Partitioning
points: What it is: splitting one logical table into smaller physical partitions inside one database server
Why it exists: a 2-billion-row table makes indexes, vacuum and deletes slow and unwieldy
Used for: time-series and log tables, multi-tenant tables and archiving old data
Strategies: range (by date), list (by region), hash (by user_id mod N)

How it works: CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint, created_at date, total int) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at); CREATE TABLE orders_2026_10 PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-01') TO ('2026-11-01'); a query with WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01' scans only that partition (partition pruning)
Benefit: pruning makes queries touch only the relevant partition
Benefit: dropping an old partition (DROP TABLE orders_2025_01) is instant, whereas DELETE of millions of rows is not
Benefit: smaller per-partition indexes fit in memory
Consider: queries that do not filter on the partition key scan every partition
Consider: a bad key creates hot partitions (everyone writes to this month), and unique constraints must include the partition key
Interview takeaway: partitioning is a single-node organization trick (vertical split by rows) and does not add machines; sharding does that

chapters.title: Replication
points: What it is: continuously copying data from one database node (primary) to one or more others (replicas)
Why it exists: one node is a single point of failure and a read bottleneck
Used for: high availability with failover, read scaling, geo-local reads and backups
How it works: the app writes to the primary, which appends to its WAL or binlog and streams it to replicas; reads go to replicas, e.g. 1 primary + 3 replicas serving 80% read traffic
Synchronous replication waits for the replica's ack before commit (no data loss, higher latency); asynchronous returns immediately (fast, but a primary crash can lose recent writes)
Topologies: single-leader (most common), multi-leader (needs conflict resolution), leaderless (Dynamo-style quorums, R + W > N)
Benefit: automatic failover keeps the service up when the primary dies
Benefit: read throughput scales by adding replicas
Consider: replication lag means a user may write and then read stale data from a replica; fix with read-your-writes (route that user to the primary)
Consider: replication adds no write capacity, since every write still lands on the primary; split-brain is a risk if two nodes both think they are primary
Interview takeaway: replication gives availability and read scale, not write scale; state the sync versus async trade-off and the lag problem

chapters.title: Sharding
points: What it is: horizontally splitting data across multiple independent database servers, each owning a subset of rows
Why it exists: when one machine cannot hold the data or handle the write load, even the biggest one, you scale out
Used for: very large systems such as social feeds, messaging and e-commerce with hundreds of millions of users
How it works: shard_id = hash(user_id) % 4. user_id 1042 -> hash % 4 = 2 -> shard 2; the router sends all of that user's queries there
Strategies: hash-based (even spread), range-based (easy range scans, risk of hot shards), directory-based lookup (flexible, extra hop)
Consistent hashing lets you add a shard and move only about 1/N of the keys, not reshuffle everything
Benefit: write and storage capacity scale almost linearly with shards
Benefit: smaller datasets per node mean faster queries and fault isolation
Consider: cross-shard joins and transactions are expensive or unsupported, so design data to be queried by the shard key
Consider: a hot key (celebrity user) overloads one shard, and resharding live data is painful
Interview takeaway: shard last, after indexing, caching, replication and partitioning are exhausted; choose the shard key by access pattern

chapters.title: Database Concepts Cheatsheet
points: Indexing: B-tree, O(log n) lookups; leftmost prefix; costs write speed and space
Transactions: BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK; keep short; single database only
ACID: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable; isolation is the tunable one
Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable; anomalies are dirty, non-repeatable, phantom
Locking: S versus X locks; pessimistic FOR UPDATE versus optimistic version column; watch deadlocks
MVCC: multiple row versions and snapshots; readers do not block writers; needs VACUUM
Connection pooling: reuse connections; size the pool deliberately; pgbouncer or HikariCP
Partitioning: split one table by range, list or hash on one server; pruning needs the key
Replication: copy via WAL; sync is safe but slow, async is fast but lossy; lag causes stale reads
Sharding: split across servers by shard key; scales writes; cross-shard queries hurt
Scaling order: index, then pool, then cache, then replicate for reads, then partition, then shard for writes
Common interview trap: replication is not sharding, and partitioning is not sharding
